blocks.content: I still remember standing in Delhi during winter mornings, feeling the heavy air around me. The fog was not just fog — it was smoke. The Air Quality Index crossed dangerous levels, and breathing itself felt difficult.

Like millions of people living in North India, I experienced the impact of stubble burning (Parali burning) every year. But instead of only complaining about pollution, one question stayed in my mind:
Can a student like me actually help solve this problem?
That question became the beginning of my project — Stubble Solution.
The Problem That Needed Urgent Attention
Every year after harvesting crops like rice and wheat, farmers face a serious challenge. They must prepare fields quickly for the next crop. Farmers generally have two options:

• Manually remove crop residue (time-consuming and expensive)
  • Burn the residue — the fastest but most harmful method
Most farmers choose burning because they lack time, machinery, or affordable alternatives. The result?

• Massive smoke emissions
  • Dangerous PM2.5 particles
  • Toxic gases spreading across cities
  • Severe winter pollution in Delhi and Northern India
  • Respiratory problems for millions of people
This problem doesn't affect only India — it exists worldwide wherever large-scale farming happens. I realized this wasn’t just an agricultural issue. It was a health crisis.
How I Got the Idea
Being from Delhi, I personally experienced pollution every winter. I saw:

• elderly people struggling to breathe,
  • children wearing masks,
  • news channels constantly discussing AQI emergencies.
Instead of blaming farmers, I tried to understand their reality. Farmers burn stubble because they need a fast solution. So my idea became clear:
👉 What if burning cannot be stopped immediately… but pollution from burning can be reduced drastically?
That thought led me to design a chemical-based pollution reduction and decomposition system.
My Journey Began — School Level Exhibition
My journey started at Rajkiya Pratibha Vikas Vidyalaya Yamuna Vihar. Our guide teacher, Ashutosh Sharma, encouraged us to participate in a science exhibition supported by institutions like:

• NCERT
  • SCERT Delhi
  • NITI Aayog

I worked on defining the problem, researching chemistry applications, and designing the concept. When our project got selected and secured 1st position at school level, it was the first moment I felt: Maybe this idea truly has potential. Our principal, Harish Kumar, motivated us to improve the model further.
Zonal Level — Facing Real Competition

The zonal competition brought together many reputed schools, including private institutions like Canterbury Public School Yamuna Vihar. Standing before judges and large audiences was intimidating. But when I explained:

• farmer challenges,
  • chemical reaction logic,
  • environmental impact,
the judges appreciated the practicality of the solution. Our project advanced again. That moment built my confidence as a presenter and innovator.
District Level — Competing with Top Schools

The district round took place at Government Boys Senior Secondary School Surajmal Vihar. Competition level increased drastically. Students from elite private schools presented advanced models. Honestly, I felt nervous. But I focused on one thing: clarity over complexity. I explained:

• the chemistry,
  • environmental science,
  • farmer usability.
After intense questioning by judges, our project achieved First Position again. That victory proved that strong ideas matter more than expensive models.
State Level — Learning Under Pressure
The state-level exhibition was massive.

• Hundreds of projects.
  • Experienced judges.
  • Limited evaluation time.

Many stalls received 20 minutes of attention, but by the time judges reached us, they had only about 3 minutes left. For a moment, I thought everything was over. Then I made a decision: I delivered the entire project explanation in crisp, powerful points. Surprisingly, the judges appreciated the clarity. Later, during announcement:
🥉 3rd Position — Ayush Paul from RPVV Yamuna Vihar
Hearing my name at the state level was unforgettable. And then came the biggest surprise. We were selected for National Level participation.
National Level — Rashtriya Bal Vaigyanik Pradarshani 2025
Our project was officially selected for: Rashtriya Bal Vaigyanik Pradarshani 2025. Hosted at: Regional Institute of Education Bhopal, Shyamla Hills, Bhopal.
My teammate Samyak Jain and I travelled together by train — my first long academic journey representing my school nationally. It was a week-long event filled with:

• student innovators from across India
  • scientific discussions
  • live presentations
  • research exposure

Although logistics were not perfect, presenting my innovation at the national stage was life-changing. We interacted with visitors, teachers, and scientists who showed genuine curiosity about solving stubble burning pollution.
Technical Explanation — How My Stubble Solution Works
My innovation combines chemical emission reduction and biological decomposition.
Phase 1 — Pre-Treatment Spray
A decomposition solution containing:

• ammonium sulfate
  • magnesium sulfate
  • calcium carbonate
  • phosphoric compounds
  • enzyme boosters (cellulase & laccase)
This softens crop residue and accelerates microbial breakdown.
Phase 2 — Pollution Control Tablet
The tablet contains compounds like:

• Calcium Oxide — captures acidic gases
  • Potassium Carbonate — catalytic oxidation
  • Iron Oxide — improves combustion efficiency
  • Ammonium Bicarbonate — reduces NOx emissions
  • Magnesium Oxide — VOC breakdown
  • Urea & Calcium Carbonate — neutralization reactions
👉 Result: Cleaner burning with drastically reduced toxic emissions.
Application Process

1. Spray decomposition solution on stubble.
  2. Allow overnight reaction.
  3. Apply tablet powder before controlled burning.
  4. Pollutants reduce significantly during combustion.
Results & Environmental Impact
Based on experimental modeling and chemical principles:

• Significant reduction in harmful gases
  • Lower smoke density
  • Improved air quality impact
  • Faster residue breakdown
  • Farmer-friendly implementation
The solution aims to reduce pollution without forcing unrealistic changes on farmers.
Challenges I Faced
This was not an easy project. Major challenges included:

• Explaining complex chemistry to non-technical audiences
  • Designing affordable solutions
  • Facing strong competition
  • Limited judging time at state level
  • Presenting confidently under pressure
I learned that innovation is not only about science — it is also about communication and psychology.
What I Learned From This Journey
This project taught me:

• Real innovation starts from real problems
  • Students can contribute to national issues
  • Confidence grows through action
  • Failure fear disappears when purpose becomes bigger
Beyond competition, I experienced new cities, travelled with teachers, explored Bhopal — the “City of Lakes,” and created memories that shaped my personality.
Future Scope of Stubble Solution
Future improvements can include:

• Large-scale field testing
  • Collaboration with agricultural universities
  • Eco-friendly commercialization
  • Integration with smart farming systems
  • Government pilot programs
My goal is to transform this student project into a real-world environmental solution.
Personal Reflection
When I started, I was just a student observing pollution. By the end of this journey, I realized something powerful:
Innovation doesn’t begin in laboratories. It begins when someone refuses to ignore a problem.
This project strengthened my identity as a student researcher and problem solver. And it is only the beginning.
SEO FAQ Section

What is stubble burning?
Stubble burning is the practice of burning leftover crop residue after harvesting to quickly prepare fields for the next crop cycle.

Why is stubble burning harmful?
It releases particulate matter, toxic gases, and smoke that significantly worsen air quality and cause respiratory diseases.

What is Ayush Paul’s Stubble Solution?
It is a chemical pre-treatment and emission-reduction tablet designed to reduce pollution released during crop residue burning.

Did this project reach national level?
Yes, the project was selected for the Rashtriya Bal Vaigyanik Pradarshani 2025, a national-level science exhibition organized under NCERT.

Can students create environmental innovations?
Absolutely. Student-led innovations often bring fresh, practical perspectives to global problems.
